properties.decision:
RULED by Anthony 2026-09-06 ("go with your above recommendations for v0.50.0"), item 4 of the v0.50.0 plan: option A with a stated convention, and option C folded in. THE CONVENTION, taught once: a relation tool whose two ends play different roles names the role end by its role (`verification_id`, `artifact_id`, `constraint_id`, `release_id`, `contributor_id`, `resource_id` …) and the other end `target_id` / `target_type`; a relation tool whose ends are peers of one kind, or where the roles are the edge's own direction, uses `from_id` / `to_id` (allocate, satisfies, provides, consumes, decomposes, depends_on, contain_component, governed_by). EVERY relation tool ALSO ACCEPTS the other family's spellings as serde aliases — `from_*`/`to_*` on the role-named tools, the role names on the from/to tools (`capability_id`/`component_id` on allocate, `capability_id`/`requirement_id` on satisfies, `component_id`/`interface_id` on provides and consumes, `parent_id`/`child_id` on decomposes and contain_component, `dependent_id`/`dependency_id` on depends_on) — and `node_id`/`node_type`, the keys search_design hands back, are accepted for the from end, which is the documented handoff failure. The schema still teaches one name (aliases are not published), `deny_unknown_fields` still catches a genuine typo, and no existing call changes meaning. Option B (rename across the surface) REJECTED as churn without capability; option D (the get_node message) is separable and cheap and stays open. A caller passing both spellings of one end is refused as a duplicate field, which is the honest answer.

WHAT WAS ON THE TABLE (recorded 2026-09-02 as brainstorming). Measured by the dev_storyflow fleet across three entries on 2026-09-02, growing each time — they reported four spellings, then six, then seven.

| tool | names the node | names the other end |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `search_design` (RETURNS) | `node_id` + `node_type` | — |
| `get_node` | `id` + `node_type` | — |
| `create_node` | `id` + `node_type` + **`props`** (nested) | — |
| `review_relations` | `node_id` + `node_type` | `other_id` + `other_type` + `incoming` |
| `authored_by` | `from_id` + `from_type` | `contributor_id` |
| `schedule_for` | `item_id` + `item_type` | `target_id` + `target_type` |
| `set_epoch_status` | `epoch_id` | — |
| `verifies` | `verification_id` | `target_type` / `target_id` |

⭐ THE SHARPEST FORM IS NOT THE COUNT, IT IS THE HANDOFF: "`search_design` hands back `node_id`; the tool you reach for next rejects that exact key." And their diagnosis of their own errors is the part worth keeping: "Every guess was informed by the tool I had used immediately before, and every one was wrong — which is the signature of an interface that is locally sensible and globally inconsistent rather than of a careless caller." Five failed calls before any of a five-idea brainstorm landed, none of them conceptual.

THE PATTERN FOR FIXING IT ALREADY EXISTED: chg:accept-1ea01d3ea7e8701a — "ContributorReq.id gains a serde alias for contributor_id. The surface still teaches one name and `deny_unknown_fields` is unchanged; no design meaning moved."

OPTIONS AS RECORDED: A — serde aliases everywhere (accept, teach one name; aliases hide the inconsistency rather than removing it). B — converge and deprecate (a consumer-facing break across 167 tools for churn). C — fix only the handoff (search_design's node_id accepted by the next tool). D — get_node's message alone (one word, `and`). E — do nothing. NOT MEASURED at the time: how many of the 167 tools differ — surveyed 2026-09-06 from the toolsnaps: 44 write tools carry two or more id/type parameters, in exactly the two families the convention names, plus the from/to pair.
properties.name: DECIDED — one convention, taught once, and the other family's names accepted as serde ALIASES on every relation tool: an asymmetric relation names its role end plus `target_*`; a symmetric one uses `from_*` / `to_*`; `node_id`/`node_type` (what search_design hands back) is accepted for the from end. No renames; nothing breaks
properties.rationale:
Recorded rather than acted on because the options span three orders of magnitude — one word in an error message, aliases on a handful of request structs, or renaming across a 167-tool surface — and the reporter's own framing ("pure interface churn — no call failed for a reason a caller could have reasoned about") argues for the cheap end while the volume of complaint argues for the expensive one.

Option D is separable from everything else here, costs one word, and would have saved a documented round trip. It does not need this question answered first.
